Hey Javier. Coming from a 280 CC, the 320 GT is a different kind of boat — more pocket cruiser than center console. Honest quick review: great-riding, efficient for its size, and the cabin genuinely works for couple weekends. If the Axopar 37 felt like too much boat, the 320 is the spot you're describing.

I broker boats, so I watch this market closely. Are you set on buying new, or open to a clean used one?

leads.name: Arto Rusanen
leads.post: Hi all! We have a 320 GTC Mk1 and some technical challenges with the front door. The door flies open on every 3rd wave. Seems like it could come from hull flex since it opens on its own more when not hitting waves head on. It happens on small waves and slower speeds(under 20kts) already. First the upper latch opens and then the lower one. On the door there are the hooks and those i have reattach with bigger screws/bolts since they got loose. Could this be a alignment issue, cable issue, latch issue? Anyone with similar challenges?
leads.flag: Mk1 320 GTC owner with a recurring, safety-adjacent door failure he's already tried to fix once himself. Frustration plus an unfixed defect is the classic upgrade seed — help now, be remembered when he's done fighting it. Also a Saxdor-literate contact inside a group full of prospects.
leads.dm:
Hey Arto. Upper latch letting go first is the useful detail — the door is peeling open from the top, which points at engagement depth more than the latches themselves.

Since the hooks already worked loose once, the geometry has probably shifted. Deepen the striker bite on the top latch first, then check the gasket — a compressed seal lets the door sit proud, and any flex does the rest. Cables usually fail one latch at a time, not in sequence.

leads.name: Allan Levitt
leads.post: On a Cruisers 4450 the air conditioner overboard goes thru a box. How do I replace the plastic thru hull. No access. Thankyou
leads.flag: 4450 owner staring down an access-nightmare repair — the moment owners quietly start weighing the fix against moving on. A concrete answer positions Zach as the guy who knows these boats; watch follow-ups for fatigue signals.
leads.dm:
Hey Allan. No access is the whole fight on that one — the fitting itself is a ten dollar part.

Two ways owners go: cut a proper inspection port near the box (makes it serviceable forever, and the next owner thanks you), or have a yard glass in a new hole nearby and cap the old run. If it sits above the waterline, you may not even need to haul.

Has anyone in the group posted photos of that spot opened up?

leads.flag: Chris has a 3650 ACMY sitting at a yard right now with the shafts pulled — an owner actively spending on the boat and facing a real decision this week, which is exactly the window to be useful. The play is a genuinely helpful answer on dripless vs. repacking (the labor overlap is the whole economics of the choice), not a pitch. Owners mid-refit are the ones who call a broker a year later, and this is the same group Rich Redmond posted in, so Zach showing up helpful twice compounds. Don't sell anything here.
leads.dm:
Hey Chris. Shafts already pulled changes the dripless math — most of the labor is money you're spending anyway, and that's usually the only time the conversion really pencils out.

If your stuffing boxes are in decent shape though, fresh packing is cheap and any yard anywhere can service it.

Is she your long-term boat, or do you see yourself moving up at some point?

leads.name: FG Hamnd
leads.post: When cruising in salt water and overnighting on moorings or at anchor for a few weeks, what do people do to flush engines and wash down the vessel after daily use ? Thanks.
leads.flag: Long-trip cruiser asking routine-maintenance questions — no transaction in sight, but exactly the profile that refers and returns. Cheap goodwill play.
leads.dm:
Hey FG. Weeks on the hook in salt is the real test of a routine.

For the engine, the flush port plus a few gallons of fresh in a collapsible jug with a small 12v pump does the job at anchor — a salt-remover concentrate stretches every gallon. For the boat itself, a pump-sprayer rinse on hardware and glass, and let the rest wait for the dock.

Cooling passages can't wait. Gelcoat can.
